title: Unravelling Multiscale Spatiotemporal Dynamics and Attribution Analysis of Evapotranspiration in a Subtropical Monsoon Basin
content:
ABSTRACT

Evapotranspiration (ET) plays a critical role in land–atmosphere interactions and ecosystem water balance. However, the component-level dynamics and controls of ET remain unclear in subtropical monsoon basins. This study integrated the SWH model, land-use transition analysis, and Geo-detector with multisource datasets to examine evaporation (E), transpiration (T), and ET in the Pearl River Basin from 1990 to 2020. Our results show that the multiyear mean annual ET was 851.89 mm, including 379.33 mm of E and 472.56 mm of T, and ET increased at 2.92 mm/a. Spatially, ET was closely coupled with T, showing ‘high-E, low-T’ patterns in urbanized coastal areas, ‘low-E, high-T’ patterns in forested interiors, and an ET depression in karst regions. Seasonally, wet-season ET was much higher than dry-season ET. E increased significantly in both seasons, with a larger contribution from the wet season, whereas T increased significantly in the dry season but declined slightly in the wet season, offsetting much of the annual T increase. Across ecosystems, water bodies had the highest E and total ET, whereas forests showed the highest T. Geo-detector analysis showed that ET variations were better explained by nonlinear interactions among vegetation, energy, and topography, with vegetation-related factors showing higher explanatory power in the dry season and energy–atmospheric factors showing higher explanatory power in the wet season. These findings improve understanding of ET partitioning under climate variability and land-use change, providing evidence for water-resource management and ecological conservation in subtropical monsoon basins.
